title: Ἵππος γέρων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 138 (= Perry 318). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γέρων ἵππος ἐπράθη πρὸς τὸ ἀλήθειν.
sentences.tr: Gerōn hippos eprathē pros to alēthein.
sentences.l: An old horse was sold for grinding.
sentences.n: ἐπράθη is the aorist passive of πιπράσκω, 'was sold'. πρός with the articular infinitive τὸ ἀλήθειν gives what he was bought for. The mill is the bottom of the world of work: what a broken animal is put to, and in Greek comedy the standing threat held over a slave.

sentences.t: Ζευχθεὶς δὲ ἐν τῷ μυλῶνι στενάζων εἶπεν· « Ἐκ ποίων δρόμων εἰς οἵους καμπτῆρας ἦλθον. »
sentences.tr: Zeuchtheis de en tōi mylōni stenazōn eipen· « Ek poiōn dromōn eis hoious kamptēras ēlthon. »
sentences.l: And having been yoked in the mill-house, groaning, he said: « From what sort of race-courses to what sort of turning-posts have I come. »
sentences.i: And yoked in the mill-house he groaned and said: « From race-courses such as those to turning-posts such as these have I come. »
sentences.n: A καμπτήρ is the post at the far end of the stadium that the chariots swing round. The horse's word for the circuit he now walks is the racetrack's word, which is the whole of his grief. ποῖος and οἷος are paired for the contrast — 'what kind … what kind'. Chambry prints a full stop, not a question mark: this is an exclamation, not a question.

sentences.t: Ὅτι μὴ λίαν ἐπαιρέσθω τις πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἀκμῆς ἢ τῆς δόξης δυνατόν· πολλοῖς γὰρ τὸ γῆρας ἐν κόποις ἀνηλώθη.
sentences.tr: Hoti mē lian epairesthō tis pros to tēs akmēs ē tēs doxēs dynaton· pollois gar to gēras en kopois anēlōthē.
sentences.l: That let no one be lifted up too much at what his prime or his repute is able to do; for with many, old age was spent in toils.
sentences.i: The story shows that no one should be lifted up too much by what his prime or his reputation can do; for many a man's old age is spent in hard labour.
sentences.n: The introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line — though here the clause holds a third-person imperative, ἐπαιρέσθω, which sits oddly under ὅτι: the moral is framed as a command with the subordinator still standing in front of it. τὸ δυνατόν with two genitives is 'what the prime, or the reputation, is able to do'. ἀνηλώθη is the aorist passive of ἀναλίσκω, 'was spent, used up' — the word for money going out; it is gnomic, stating what happens as a rule, which the idiomatic line carries with an English present. πολλοῖς is the dative of the persons in whose case it happens.
